title: the seasons
hook: the fan comes down from the top shelf and the heavy blanket goes up; Ayurveda reads the year the way it read the day

segments.voice: Yesterday we closed the daily routine, dinacharya: the day's joints, the twilights, and a round that bends to the person keeping it. Which joint of your day got a breath? Day one thousand three hundred.

The fan comes down from the top shelf. The heavy blanket goes up in its place. Soup drops off the menu at home, and something cold shows up instead. Nobody holds a meeting about it. A household just shifts, a little at a time, as the weather turns. That quiet shifting is what the next part of the classical texts is about. They've walked through the day. Now they zoom out and read the whole year the same way, as a round with its own turns. Today: the seasons.
screen: `THE FAN COMES DOWN.` → `A HOUSEHOLD SHIFTS QUIETLY.` → `THE YEAR, READ LIKE THE DAY.`

segments.voice: The Sanskrit word for a season is ritu, and the seasonal routine is ritucharya, the conduct of the season, a twin to dinacharya, the conduct of the day. In its chapter on the seasons, the Charaka Samhita makes a plain promise, paraphrased: a person who knows what suits each season, in food and in activity, grows in strength and in complexion. So the seasons aren't scenery. They're something a body lives through, and something to keep step with. Then a surprise for anyone raised on four seasons. The Ashtanga Hridaya divides the year into six. Shishira, the cold late winter. Vasanta, spring. Grishma, summer. Varsha, the rains. Sharad, the clear autumn after the rains. And hemanta, the early winter. In this reckoning the rains are a season of their own, not a footnote. So the year becomes a bigger day. The same eye that noticed dawn and dusk now notices the turn from heat to rain. And the seasons outside meet the qualities inside. The doshas, described through hot and cold, dry and oily, light and heavy, rise and settle with the weather, and the texts suggest meeting each season with its opposite. It's also local. A person in a snowy city or a desert town will have a different year from the one the texts describe. The lesson that travels isn't the six names. It's the habit of asking, as the weather turns: what does this season need from me? We'll take the year apart, a piece at a time, in the days ahead.
screen: `RITUCHARYA: THE CONDUCT OF THE SEASON` · `KNOW WHAT SUITS EACH SEASON` · `SIX SEASONS, THE RAINS AMONG THEM` · `WHAT DOES THIS SEASON NEED?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read today's season in your body. Start with the air. Notice the air on the skin: warm, cool, damp, dry? Notice the light where you are. Then turn inward. Does the body feel heavy or light this week? Hungry or not? Sleepy, restless, steady? No fixing. Just a weather report from the inside, to sit beside the one outside. Then rest in the breath, whatever the season. If you pray, you can give thanks for the season you're in. The bell holds the time.
The seasons. Ritu, a season, and ritucharya, the conduct that keeps step with it. In the Ashtanga Hridaya, the year turns six times. Today's word.
Your line: the seasons. Today, step outside for a minute, read the weather the way you'd read a face, and ask what this season needs from you. Day one thousand three hundred.

howItsDone: People who follow Ayurveda adjust food, sleep and activity through ritucharya, the seasonal routine, which the Ashtanga Hridaya lays out across six seasons including the rains.

ask what this season needs, in food and in activity.

original.note: Sanskrit ritucharya: ritu, season, and charya, conduct. The seasonal routine of the classical Ayurvedic texts.

trapdoor: what you thought: seasons are just the weather outside.
what it means: ritucharya treats the year like a bigger day, a round to keep step with in food and activity.
what a scholar hears: the Ashtanga Hridaya's six ritus, shishira through hemanta, with the rains as a season of their own.

sources.ref: Charaka Samhita, Sutrasthana 6.3 (strength and complexion grow for one who knows what suits each season in food and activity)
Ashtanga Hridaya, Sutrasthana 3.1–2 (the year in six seasons: shishira, vasanta, grishma, varsha, sharad, hemanta)

notes: First of the seasons days (1300 onward). This day introduces ritu, ritucharya and the six seasons; 1301 takes the two halves of the year (adana and visarga). Later days can take individual seasons.
Charaka Sutrasthana 6.3 (tasyashitiyadyad aharad balam varnash ca vardhate, yasyartusatmyam viditam ceshtaharavyapashrayam) recalled from memory; confirm verse and paraphrase.

Ashtanga Hridaya Sutrasthana 3 season list and order (shishira, vasanta, grishma in one half; varsha, sharad, hemanta in the other): confirm. 'The year ... turns six times' is drawn from the text's division; the teach no longer explains why there are six.
English glosses for the seasons (late winter, early winter, clear autumn) are approximate; confirm.
